source_read: PMC full text PMC6559129 in my own browser tab (title checked): abstract, Introduction, both subsections of Investigation and Classification of Overdose Deaths, all four subsections of Epidemiologic Analysis, Death Certificates Remain the Core (with initiatives I to VII), Conclusions, acknowledgements, conflict-of-interest and ethics statements, author affiliations (collapsed panel read with javascript on my tab), and all 95 references with their annotations. Fig. 1 is a flowchart: legend read, image not viewed (no values are taken from it). No tables, no supplement. No funding statement found on the page. Card check only (task has no claims; step 1 empty).

design.note: Narrative review (Current Epidemiology Reports, Topical Collection on Injury Epidemiology); no search strategy or selection criteria. 95 references confirmed; 11 references carry the 'of major importance' mark in the body citations (10, 11, 12, 15, 31, 32, 33, 41, 42, 55, 58; the reference list itself prints the mark on only 5 of them); 12 visible self-citations confirmed (refs 14, 15, 32, 41, 42, 45, 52, 53, 62, 77, 85, 92), 4 of them among the 11 (15, 32, 41, 42).

instrument.note: none-applicable with the editors' narrative-review checklist (METHODS 5.3).

key_findings.note: Introduction, single paragraph: data generated by multiple agencies and actors, no single agency with quality-control oversight of the whole process (Fig. 1).
MDI subsection, 1st and 2nd paragraphs. The source adds that ME/Cs complete the medical part for deaths over which they assumed jurisdiction.
6th paragraph; ref 34 is the NFLIS 2017 medical examiner/coroner office survey report (August 2018); no response rate given in the review.
7th paragraph (refs 27, 32 for the listing rule; ref 35 for Gill).
Death Certificate ICD-10 Coding, 1st paragraph; 'whether or not the drug was given in a treatment setting'.

1st paragraph (92/71/73/62%, ref 10 = Warner et al., Acad Forensic Pathol 2013) and 4th paragraph (85% Maryland, >40% Utah, 8% national; 2016 range 1% Connecticut and Massachusetts to 68% Maryland, from CDC WONDER, ref 44, not Warner).
3rd paragraph: 4.7 to 9.3 per 100,000; 57.7% to 94.4%; January 2014 process; personal correspondence; gabapentin 2.9% (2013) to 17% (2014) after routine testing from July 2014 (ref 45).

Methodologic Considerations 5th paragraph (R99; ref 49) and Statistical Adjustment 4th paragraph (lag longer than for natural deaths or suicides, usually toxicology delays; NCHS regression models for provisional completeness).
1st and 2nd paragraphs; neither '20%' sentence carries a citation.
1st to 3rd paragraphs. Recomputed: 12.46/10.31 = 1.209, i.e. 21% higher. Buchanich (ref 41) is a co-author.
1st and 2nd paragraphs. The source says heroin-specific analytes go undetected because heroin is rapidly metabolized to 6-AM and 6-AM to morphine; the card's wording is a fair compression.

3rd and 4th paragraphs. 'Linked certificates with post-mortem toxicology' is supported by the title of ref 62 (Slavova, Bunn et al., 2017, linking certificates, toxicology and prescription history), not by the review's sentence itself; the denominator is indeed not stated.
7th paragraph: 32 states, 2016 to 2017; at least 60% of September 2017 supplemental funding mandated for ME/Cs; SUDORS limited to unintentional opioid overdose deaths.
2nd paragraph (75, 76, 78, 81, 83, 85%, 2011 to 2016; ref 87), 3rd paragraph (32% computerized, networked; ref 34) and Conclusions.

reporting_issues.note: Both '20%' statements are uncited. In the same NCHS series the review quotes, 20% unspecified matches 2013 to 2014 (78% to 81% specified), so the figure is probably dated rather than invented; the consequence (cite the dated series) stands.

Personal correspondence (3rd paragraph) and the 75% / '51–75%' figures without response rate (6th paragraph) confirmed. The figures also imply that offices 'always' request testing for other opioids more often than for fentanyl and heroin, which the review leaves unexplained.
'undermined intent' (Methodologic Considerations, 4th paragraph); 'commision' (ref 3), 'discusse' (ref 45), 'etimates' (ref 49), 'involed' and 'acurate' (ref 87) all present.

risk_of_bias.note: Overall high (no systematic search) follows the worst-domain rule. One domain note needs correcting: the balance domain says over-attribution is mentioned only in Gill's remark, but the review also reports the SAMHSA panel's distinction between 'drug-caused' and 'drug-detected' deaths (MDI subsection, 4th paragraph), the rule that non-contributing drugs should not be recorded (7th paragraph) and NAME's call to interpret toxicology in the context of the circumstances (3rd paragraph). The judgment (some concerns) still fits: none of these is quantified.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor. Gap (1) is weak: the abstract's claim that text tools improve specific-opioid quantification is compatible with the body's statement that they cannot reach certificates naming no drug.

missed: Correction (funding.affiliations_note): four authors are at the University of Kentucky (Slavova, Delcher, Bunn, Costich), not five; with Buchanich (Pittsburgh) and Goldberger (Florida) the article has six authors.

Correction (design_detail): Goldberger's printed affiliation is the Department of Pathology, Immunology and Laboratory Medicine, College of Medicine, University of Florida; 'forensic toxicology' describes his field, and his role as co-chair of the SAMHSA panel is not stated in this article (it may come from the Goldberger 2013 card).

Missed finding relevant to 'involved' versus 'caused': the three recommendation papers. The SAMHSA consensus panel distinguished 'drug-caused' from 'drug-detected' deaths and said non-uniform classification undermines incidence and prevalence data; NAME called for a complete scene investigation, a comprehensive toxicology panel interpreted in the context of the circumstances, all responsible substances listed by generic name, and 'accident' as the manner for opioid misuse without apparent intent of self-harm, keeping 'undetermined' for rare cases where evidence supports more than one intent; OSAC named three essential initiatives (MDI subsection, 3rd to 5th paragraphs; Methodologic Considerations, 4th paragraph).

Missed finding: the relayed CSTE Overdose Subcommittee recommendation that jurisdictions be compared on total drug overdose death rates, and that drug-specific trends remain useful only while the degree of drug specification does not vary markedly from year to year (Methodologic Considerations, 2nd paragraph).

Minor: Ruhm's state-level adjusted rates (2008 to 2014) varied widely with the share of unspecified deaths, and the authors note predictive models could add ME/C jurisdiction type and toxicology protocols but such data are not readily available (Statistical Adjustment, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs). The replication timeline's Garnett 2026 entry is not from this source and was not checked here.
